headline: Golden Toilet Thief Admits He Used the £4.75m Loo the Day Before It Vanished. His Review: Splendid
dek: An 18-carat gold toilet was ripped out of Winston Churchill's birthplace in five minutes. It has never been seen again.
body: It was called America. It was a fully working toilet made of solid 18-carat gold, weighing about 98 kilograms and insured for £4.75 million. And one day it was simply gone.

The toilet, created by Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan, was plumbed in and ready for use as part of an exhibition at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, the birthplace of Winston Churchill. Visitors could book a slot and use it.

Before dawn on September 14, 2019, a gang rammed two stolen vehicles through the palace's locked wooden gates, smashed through a window and a door, and tore the toilet out of the floor. The whole raid took about five minutes.

At the trial in 2025, one 39-year-old defendant admitted he had visited the palace the day before the heist and used the golden toilet. Asked in court what the experience was like, he gave a one-word review.

His phone told a less innocent story. It held photos of the toilet, a selfie with it, a picture of the cubicle lock, and the very window later smashed in the raid. He claimed he had been photographing flags in the distance and simply thought the lock was funny.

The jury was not convinced, and he was convicted of burglary. The ringleader, who had pleaded guilty, got four more years on top of a near 20-year sentence for other crimes. The man who called it splendid got 27 months. The judge called the heist bold and brazen.
None of the gold has ever been found. Prosecutors believe it was cut up and sold, which means somewhere out there, someone may be wearing jewellery made from a toilet.

headline: Raccoon Breaks Into Liquor Store, Drinks the Scotch Shelf Dry, Passes Out in the Bathroom
dek: Staff opened up on Saturday morning to smashed bottles, a whisky lake on the floor and one very unconscious masked burglar.
body: Some people end a long week at the bar. One raccoon in Virginia decided to skip the bar entirely and go straight to the warehouse.

Overnight into Saturday, November 29, the animal broke into a closed, state-run Virginia ABC liquor store near Ashland in Hanover County. Investigators believe it came in through the roof: a ceiling tile gave way, and the raccoon came down with it.

What happened next was less a burglary and more a bender. The raccoon headed straight for the bottom shelf, home of the scotch and whisky, and started knocking bottles over. Glass shattered. Liquor pooled across the floor. Security cameras captured the aftermath, which looked roughly like a frat party with fewer witnesses.

body.quote: The county's animal control officer said the raccoon had drunk nearly everything it could reach.

body: When an employee arrived the next morning, the culprit was not hiding or fleeing. It was lying flat out on the bathroom floor, completely unconscious.

Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter collected the suspect and, in a rare act of mercy toward a burglar, simply let it sleep it off. After a few hours of rest it had no injuries at all, except what staff described as a probable hangover.

The shelter later joked online about the raccoon's poor life choices and said it hoped the animal had learned that breaking and entering is wrong. Once sober, the raccoon was released back into the wild with no charges filed and, presumably, a pounding headache.

headline: Beavers Finish Government's 7-Year Dam Project Overnight, Save Taxpayers $1.2 Million
dek: Officials spent years on permits and land talks. A family of rodents spent a couple of nights on it and did a better job.
location: Brdy Protected Landscape Area, Czech Republic
body: Every government has a project that seems to take forever. In the Czech Republic, one of them was finally finished, and not by anyone on the payroll.

Conservation officials had wanted to build barriers near the Klabava River, on a former army training ground south-west of Prague that became a protected area in 2016. The goal was to shield the river, and its critically endangered crayfish, from sediment and acidic water draining out of two nearby ponds, and to create a wetland along the way.

The plan was drawn up in 2018. It was approved. It had a budget of about 30 million koruna, roughly $1.2 million. And then it sat there for years, stuck in negotiations over land and permits between military forest managers and the river basin authority.

Before a single excavator arrived, a local beaver family of around eight animals took matters into their own paws. They built at least four dams across a drainage gully soldiers had once dug, with more under construction.

The resulting network of pools and channels covers about twice the area the human planners had in mind. The head of the protected-area administration said the beavers had created the habitat almost overnight, with no paperwork and at no cost, saving the state the entire 30 million crowns.

body.quote: A zoologist pointed out the key difference: beavers can build a dam in a night or two, while people need permits and funding first.

body: Officials said they do not expect any conflict with their new unpaid contractors for at least a decade. The nearest farmland that could be affected is far from the site. The beavers have not submitted an invoice.

headline: Cops Disguise Themselves as a Dancing Lion to Pounce on Burglar Who Robbed a Police Chief 3 Times
dek: He always ran when he saw officers. He did not run from a giant papier-mache lion at a temple fair.
body: Thai police had a problem. Their suspect, a serial burglar, had a simple strategy: every time he spotted an officer, he ran. So the officers stopped looking like officers. They started looking like a lion.

The man was accused of breaking into the Bangkok home of a local police commander not once, not twice, but three times in early February 2026. The haul was worth about 2 million baht, roughly $64,000, and included Buddhist amulets and artifacts, among them two foot-tall Buddha statues.

Investigators followed the trail of stolen amulets he had sold and learned he liked to visit temples in Nonthaburi province, on the edge of Bangkok. After weeks of surveillance, they came up with a plan worthy of a heist movie.

On February 18, at a Lunar New Year temple fair, plainclothes officers joined a lion dance procession hidden inside a red-and-yellow lion costume. As the 33-year-old suspect wandered through the festivities, the lion slowly danced its way toward him.

body.quote: Then the officer holding the lion's head lunged, and the lion pinned the burglar to the ground.

body: Colleagues rushed in to help, and Thailand's Metropolitan Police Bureau proudly released photos and video of what may be the most festive arrest in history.
Police said the man confessed and told them he stole to fund gambling and drugs. He already had prior convictions for theft. He also, presumably, now has a lifelong fear of parades.

headline: Thieves Steal 12 Tonnes of KitKats, All 413,793 Bars, and Vanish Without a Trace
dek: Nestlé says the criminals took its slogan too literally. The chocolate is still out there.
body: For decades, KitKat has told the world to have a break. Somewhere in Europe, a gang of thieves decided to have 413,793 of them.

Nestlé announced that a truck carrying about 12 tonnes of KitKat bars had been stolen on its way from the company's production site in central Italy to Poland. The chocolate was meant for shops across Europe. It never arrived.
To make it even more absurd, the stolen bars came from KitKat's new Formula 1 range, shaped like tiny racing cars. The thieves made a clean getaway, which feels appropriate.

body.quote: In its statement, KitKat said the criminals had taken its famous slogan too literally, and praised their exceptional taste.

body: When the company went public, neither the truck nor its sweet cargo had been found, and no arrests had been reported. Nobody was hurt.

Nestlé has turned every chocolate fan into a detective. Each bar carries a batch code, and shoppers, shops and wholesalers can scan it to see whether their snack is from the stolen load. If it matches, they get instructions for alerting the company.

The company said the bars are perfectly safe to eat and that it was going public to highlight a real problem: cargo theft is on the rise for businesses of every size. Somewhere, someone is sitting on half a million chocolate racing cars and wondering what to do next.

headline: Couple Accidentally Mails Their Cat to Amazon in a Box of Boots. She Survives 6 Days and 600 Miles
dek: The returns warehouse opened the package expecting steel-toed boots. It found a calico instead.
location: Lehi, Utah to Jurupa Valley, California, USA
body: Every cat owner knows cats love boxes. One family in Utah learned exactly how far that love can take a cat: about 630 miles.

On April 10, 2024, a man in Lehi, Utah, packed five pairs of steel-toed work boots back into a large box to return them to Amazon. What he did not notice was Galena, the family's six-year-old indoor calico and a well-known box enthusiast, who had quietly climbed in with them.
The box was sealed and shipped. The family spent the next week searching for their cat, putting up posters and posting appeals on social media, with no idea she was riding UPS across state lines.

On April 16, a worker at an Amazon returns warehouse in Jurupa Valley, California, opened the box and found a cat where the boots should have been. An off-duty employee who rescues cats on the side came in with food and a carrier and took her home.

Galena had spent roughly six days in the box with no food or water. A vet found her a little thinner and mildly dehydrated but otherwise fine, with normal bloodwork. Her microchip led the vet straight to her owners, who at first assumed the phone call was a prank.

body.quote: The owners credited three small miracles: a split seam that let in air, mild weather, and the warehouse worker who took her in.

body: The couple flew to California for the reunion, then drove about ten hours home with Galena. Their advice to other pet owners: get your pets microchipped, and triple-check your Amazon boxes.

headline: Officials Beg Fans to Respect the Privacy of Neil, a 1-Ton Seal Who Fights Parked Cars
dek: He bends bollards, smashes barriers and lies in the road. He also has more TikTok followers than Tasmania has people.
body: Most celebrities ask for privacy after a scandal. Neil has had a dozen scandals, and he is a seal, so officials are asking on his behalf.

Neil is a five-year-old male southern elephant seal weighing around 1,000 kilograms, about as much as a small car. Twice a year, after months of feeding at sea, he hauls himself ashore for a tour of beachside towns in southern Tasmania. His latest visit was his twelfth.
His TikTok following of 1.4 million is more than double Tasmania's entire human population. His criminal record is similarly impressive.

Over his visits, Neil has bent traffic bollards, damaged a sign warning the public about seals, flattened a fence he tried to vault, picked fights with parked cars and smashed through barriers built specifically to keep him off the roads. He enjoys lying in the middle of the street, occasionally bringing an entire town to a halt, and keeps returning to a favourite sidewalk puddle even after rangers relocate him.

At a news conference in Hobart, a state wildlife official asked fans to give Neil some space, calling his fame a double-edged sword. He warned that people risk loving Neil to death, and asked the public to stop revealing which town the seal is currently in.

body.quote: A seal scientist explained that young males practise for adult dominance battles. With no rivals around, Neil practises on cars.

body: Some fans online have embraced him as an anti-authority hero. A local resident called him one of the area's biggest exports. If he reaches adulthood, Neil could grow to about five metres long and triple his weight, which is bad news for the bollards.

headline: Court Rules a Fart Is Not Free Speech After Man Deliberately Lets One Rip at Police
dek: He was fined €500. He appealed on free-expression grounds. The judge was not moved.
body: Some legal battles define a nation's values. This one was about a fart.

On June 5, 2020, police in a Vienna park stopped a man sitting on a bench with friends for a routine ID check. According to police, he rose slightly from the bench, looked the officers straight in the eye, and released what they described as a massive fart.

Vienna police fined him €500 for offending public decency. They explained on Twitter that nobody gets fined for an accidental toot, but this man had already been provocative and uncooperative earlier that day. They added, drily, that their officers do not much enjoy being farted at.

The man fought the fine. In April 2021, Vienna's administrative court reduced it to €100 because of his clean record and finances. But the judge firmly rejected his argument that the fart was a protected form of expression.

body.quote: Farts and burps, the ruling said, have no communicative content, and even if they did, they would go beyond the bounds of decency.

body: The court record described in loving detail how he lifted his buttocks before letting go, while his friends laughed and he grinned at the officers.

His lawyer insisted it was either unintentional or free speech, and vowed to take the matter all the way to Austria's Constitutional Court on principle. The rest of us are left to wonder what the founding fathers of Austrian law would have made of it.

img.alt: An autumn path lined with park benches and golden trees in Vienna

headline: Man Accused of Swapping $34,000 of LEGO for Pasta. Police Say His Plan Got Cooked Al Dente
dek: He allegedly bought LEGO sets, kept the pieces, filled the boxes with dried pasta and returned them. At least 70 times.
body: Some people build LEGO. One man allegedly built a pasta-based retail scheme so elaborate it deserves its own instruction booklet.

Police in Irvine, California, arrested a 28-year-old man from nearby Paramount on suspicion of grand theft. According to investigators, his method was simple. Buy expensive LEGO sets at Target. Take out the minifigures and valuable pieces. Fill the boxes back up with dried pasta so they weigh about the same. Return them for a full refund.
Police say he pulled it off at least 70 times at Target stores across the country, racking up around $34,000 in losses.
Irvine detectives eventually set up surveillance at a local Target, identified their man and arrested him at the store, all captured on officers' body cameras.
The department then released photos of the recovered evidence: piles of LEGO figures, including Star Wars characters, alongside bags of durum wheat semolina pasta allegedly used as stand-ins.

body.quote: On Facebook, police called it a bad build and warned that any master plan swapping LEGOs for linguine will end up cooked al dente.

body: He was booked into Orange County Jail. Target has not said whether it plans to start weighing its returns more carefully, or simply start checking them for spaghetti.

img.alt: A colourful jumble of assorted LEGO bricks

headline: Orcas Bring Back 1987's Hottest Fashion Trend: Wearing Dead Salmon as Hats
dek: A killer whale was photographed with a fish balanced on its head, reviving a mystery that has baffled scientists for nearly 40 years.
body: Fashion is cyclical, and apparently that applies to killer whales too.

On October 25, 2024, a photographer near Point No Point in Puget Sound captured a male orca swimming along with a dead salmon perched neatly on top of his head. The nonprofit Orca Network reported the sighting, and researchers identified the whale as J27, nicknamed Blackberry, a 32-year-old male from J pod.
J pod belongs to the endangered southern resident killer whales, a population of about 71 animals split into three pods that eat nothing but fish. And they have a history with this particular look.

body.h2: The summer of the salmon hat

body: In 1987, a female in K pod started wearing salmon on her head. Within months, the trend had spread to the other two pods. Then, almost as suddenly as it began, it vanished, and it was barely seen again for decades.

The new sighting came during an unusually big chum salmon run, the same week J pod spent a rare ten days in a row being spotted in the area. That may matter, because nobody actually knows why orcas do this. Theories include playing with spare food, saving a snack for later, or some kind of social food-sharing.

body.quote: One biologist summed up the science honestly: it is all speculation.

body: She has seen southern residents wear the look four or five times since 2005, and says it at least suggests a whale with plenty to eat. Other experts are not ready to call a full comeback. One photo, they note, does not make a trend. Fashion critics in the Pacific Northwest remain divided.

headline: Man Facing Car-Theft Charges Drives a Stolen Car to His Own Car-Theft Hearing
dek: An auto theft task force watched him park. He never made it in front of the judge.
body: There are bad ideas, and then there is driving a stolen car to court for your stolen-car case.

A 41-year-old man from Soledad, California, was due to appear at the Monterey County courthouse in Salinas on a pending auto theft charge. At around 11 a.m. on Tuesday, March 24, 2026, he pulled into the courthouse parking area, on time and ready to face the music.
The car he arrived in had been reported stolen in San Jose.

As luck would have it for everyone except him, members of a regional auto theft task force, known as MADCAT, were watching as he parked. Of all the parking lots in California, he had picked the one where car-theft specialists were literally on duty.

body.quote: Deputies met him right outside the courtroom where his car-theft case was about to be heard.

body: He was arrested before he could set foot in front of the judge. The sheriff's office said the arrest went smoothly.

He was booked into Monterey County Jail on suspicion of unlawfully taking a vehicle, committing a felony while out on bail, and driving on a suspended licence. His original case is presumably now the least of his problems.

headline: Fugitive Otter 841 Keeps Stealing Surfboards and Outsmarting Wildlife Officials
dek: Nets, traps and a decoy surfboard all failed. Santa Cruz's most wanted sea otter just dived off and kept going.
body: Surfers off Santa Cruz spent the summer of 2023 dealing with an unusual hazard. Not sharks, not rip currents, but a five-year-old sea otter with a surfboard habit.

Known officially as Otter 841, the female southern sea otter developed a routine: swim up to a surfer, climb aboard, refuse to leave, and start biting the board. In one case she chewed off part of a board's nose.
Crime may run in the family. Otter 841 was born in captivity and released into the wild in June 2020, and her mother had also been captured for harassing kayakers.

Teams from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Monterey Bay Aquarium spent weeks trying to catch her. They towed a baited surfboard toward their boat. They tried several kinds of nets. They deployed an underwater trap operated by divers.
Every time they got close, she simply dived off and swam away. Officials could not net her in open water, and sedating her was off the table because she could drown.

body.quote: A local photographer said the failed capture attempts had become almost comical.

body: Federal wildlife officials called her behaviour highly unusual and suggested hormones or people feeding her might be to blame. Meanwhile, she gained a fan club that gathered on the cliffs every day to watch. No humans were hurt, and as of late July she was still at large. Southern sea otters, once down to about 50 animals in 1938, now number around 3,000. At least one of them is very good at surfing.

headline: It's Official: A Judge Has Ruled That Tacos and Burritos Are Sandwiches
dek: A strip-mall rule said sandwiches only. A taco shop owner fought it for two years, and won.
body: The internet has argued for years about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. In Indiana, a court has settled a far bolder question.

The owner of a local restaurant called The Famous Taco wanted to open a second location in a Fort Wayne strip mall. There was one problem. The plaza was bound by an agreement with a neighbouring condo association that allowed only a sandwich-bar-style restaurant selling made-to-order, subway-style sandwiches. No alcohol. No outdoor seating. And, everyone assumed, no tacos.
The rule was reportedly designed to keep national fast-food chains out. When the local plan commission refused to amend it to explicitly allow tacos and burritos, the owner sued.

body.h2: The ruling heard round the lunch hour

body: After more than two years of legal back and forth, Allen Superior Court Judge Craig Bobay delivered his verdict in May 2024.

body.quote: Tacos and burritos, the judge wrote, are Mexican-style sandwiches.

body: Because the agreement never said the sandwiches had to be American-style, the judge concluded the taco shop had been allowed all along, and the whole fight to amend it had been unnecessary.
The owner said he was relieved and expected the new location to open within a few months. The hot dog question, sadly, remains open.
